'''''Araujia sericifera''''' is a [[perennial plant|perennial]] [[vine|vining]] plant in the genus ''[[Araujia]]'', of the family [[Apocynaceae]], that is native to [[South America]].<ref name="North Carolina">{{cite web|url=https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/araujia-sericifera/|title=''Araujia sericifera''|work=Plant Toolbox|publisher=North Carolina Cooperative Extension|access-date=March 8, 2024|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240207064303/https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/araujia-sericifera/|archive-date=February 7, 2024|url-status=live}}</ref> The species was described in 1817 by the [[Portuguese people|Portuguese]] botanist [[Félix de Avelar Brotero]]. The synonym ''Araujia hortorum'' is in more frequent use in New Zealand.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.terrain.net.nz/friends-of-te-henui-group/weeds/moth-plant-araujia-sericifera.html|title=T.E.R.R.A.I.N ''Araujia hortorum'' (mothplant) |website=T.E.R.R.A.I.N |accessdate=14 May 2017}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.landcareresearch.co.nz/__data/assets/pdf_file/0007/77911/Ecology_pest_status_moth_plant_Araujia_hortorum.pdf |title=Ecology and pest status of moth plant, Arajia hortorum |website=Landcare Research }}</ref> Its common names include '''bladderflower''', '''white bladderflower''', '''bladder vine''', '''cruel vine''', '''cruel plant''', '''moth plant''', '''moth vine''', '''common moth vine''', and '''false choko'''.<ref name="North Carolina"/> 

It was introduced to Europe and other areas as an ornamental plant, but it is now considered a [[noxious weed]]. In some countries, such as France, the attractive and abundant fragrant flowering make it a specimen considered worth cultivating. However its strong robustness combined with high seed production can make it invasive in most environments, but not in France due to its sensitivity to frost.

==Etymology==
The genus name (''Araujia'') derives from [[António de Araújo e Azevedo, 1st Count of Barca]] (1754–1817), a Portuguese amateur botanist who conducted scientific studies and experiments in his own botanical garden. The species' Latin name ''sericifera'' means "silk-bearing" and refers to the silky hairs surrounding the seeds inside the fruits. ''Araujia sericofera'' is an incorrect [[Synonym (taxonomy)|taxonomic synonym]] for ''Araujia sericifera''.<ref>[https://www.itis.gov/servlet/SingleRpt/SingleRpt?search_topic=TSN&search_value=500960#null Integrated Taxonomic Information System Report]</ref><ref>The Plant List (2013). Version 1.1. Published on the Internet; http://www.theplantlist.org/ (accessed October 2016)</ref><ref>{{cite book|title=The Jepson Manual: Higher Plants Of California|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=wAyG5J_7uOAC&q=Araujia+sericofera%22the+jepson+manual%22&pg=PA171 |publisher=University of California Press|accessdate=September 13, 2014|isbn = 9780520082557|year = 1993}}</ref>

==Description==
[[Image:Araujia sericifera flower.JPG|left|220px|thumb|Closeup of flowers]]
[[Image:Araujia sericifera 5.jpg|left|220px|thumb|As an ornamental plant]]
''Araujia sericifera'' is a creeping vine that can climb up to {{convert|5|-|10|m}} high. When broken it releases a milky, smelly exudate. Leaves are opposite, dark green, glossy and quite fleshy, almost triangular, with entire margins, about {{convert|10|-|12|cm}} long and {{convert|1|-|6|cm}} wide with an intact leaf margin. The upper side is dark green, bare and shiny, the underside is grey-green with felt-like hairs. When a stem, leaf or unripe fruit is broken, a white milky juice is produced at the breaking point. It is slightly toxic and can cause an allergic [[skin reaction]] when touched. 

The stems are thin and right-winding. They branch strongly and can lignify at the base. The plant usually wraps itself around other plants or around a post or the bars of a fence. The root system consists of a short [[taproot]] with superficial [[lateral root]]s. The plant's stems and leaves may senesce in late summer or early autumn, but new shoots will grow on the old stems as climbing support.

===Inflorescences===
The twining stems feature scented, cup-shaped bisexual flowers, around {{convert|2|cm}} in width, with five white, cream-coloured, violet or pale pink petals. The flowers are generally pollinated by moths (hence the name "moth plant"), butterflies and bees ([[entomophily]]), but they can self-pollinate. The flowering period extends from late spring to summer. The flowers of Araujia sericifera resemble those of ''[[Stephanotis floribunda]]'' in some respects, a vine that also belongs to the dogbane family.

The pear-shaped fruits are large pods, about {{convert|8|-|10|cm}} long. They contain many black seeds attached to silky hairs that enable them to be distributed by the wind. The fruits outwardly resemble those of [[chayote]] or choko (''Sechium edule''), hence the name ''false choko''.

===Insect trap===
The structure of the flower includes a number of wedge-shaped openings that function as an [[insect trap]] (hence its English name of "cruel plant"), without being a [[carnivorous plant]], where it occasionally and inadvertently traps the pollinator's [[proboscis]], leading to its death. When the foragers put their tongue in the flower, it is blocked by hooks and only the most robust insects manage to free themselves. The insects can die in the flower if the captivity lasts too long. The [[hummingbird hawk-moth]], [[monarch butterfly]], and some bees are often victims of this plant.

==Distribution==
The plant is native to South America: Peru mainly, but also Argentina, Brazil, and Uruguay. 

It was introduced to Europe and other areas as an ornamental plant, but it is now considered a [[noxious weed]]. The plant is now widely distributed in France by horticultural networks as a climbing and scent plant. It thrives in rich soil in sunny locations (possibly also in partial shade) and becomes perennial when protected from frost. The plant's geographical distribution included southern Europe, [[South Africa]], North America ([[California]], [[Georgia (U.S. state)|Georgia]], [[North Carolina]]), South America ([[Argentina]], [[Brazil]], [[Paraguay]], [[Uruguay]]), [[Australia]], and [[New Zealand]] in 2024.<ref name="North Carolina"/><ref>[http://www.rnzih.org.nz/pages/araujiasericifera.htm Araujia sericifera - moth plant], Royal New Zealand Institute of Horticulture. Copied from Ian Popay, Paul Champion & Trevor James, ''An Illustrated Guide to Common Weeds of New Zealand''. {{ISBN|0-473-09760-5}}.</ref><ref name=PWO/>

==Habitat==
These plants grow in wastelands with trees and hedges, in forests and in rocky places or cliffs. They prefer sunny or partially shady places, at an altitude of {{convert|0|-|1800|m}} above sea level.

The fast-growing vines can cover a tree canopy in two or three years, competing with the tree for light, water, and nutrients. They damage trees by this competition and by twining so tightly around their branches that it [[girdling|girdles]] them.<ref>CDFA [https://www.cdfa.ca.gov/PHPPS/IPC/weedinfo/araujia.htm EncycloWeedia].</ref>

==Butterflies==
The plant can be used as an alternative food source for [[caterpillar]]s of the [[monarch butterfly]].<ref>{{cite web |url= http://nzbutterfly.info/resident/monarch/food.htm| title=Alternative Monarch foodplants| date=5 March 2009| publisher=nzButterfly.info| accessdate=February 8, 2013}}</ref><ref>{{cite web| url=http://www.sciencelearn.org.nz/Science-Stories/Butterflies/Monarch-butterflies |publisher=Sciencelearn Hub| title=Monarch butterflies| accessdate=February 8, 2013}}</ref> Although monarch caterpillars are not known to occur naturally on the plant, they will readily feed on leaves when supplies of ''[[Gomphocarpus physocarpus]]'' (swan plant) have run out.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Wise|first1=K. A. J.|author-link1=Keith Arthur John Wise|date=June 1963|url=https://nzetc.victoria.ac.nz/tm/scholarly/tei-Bio11Tuat02-t1-body-d5.html|title=Food-Plants of 'Monarch' Butterfly Larvae|journal=Tuatara|volume=11|number=2|pages=81-82|location=[[Wellington|Wellington, New Zealand]]|publisher=[[Victoria University of Wellington]]|access-date=March 7, 2024|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231130120728/https://nzetc.victoria.ac.nz/tm/scholarly/tei-Bio11Tuat02-t1-body-d5.html|archive-date=November 30, 2023|url-status=live}}</ref>

==Toxicity==
Moth plant is toxic for some people. Skin contact with its sap can cause rashes. Contact with the eyes, in particular, can cause severe discomfort.
